claim: Missense mutations in OGT have been linked to intellectual disability.
source: Recently, missense mutations in OGT have been linked to intellectual disability, indicating that this modification is important for the development and functioning of the nervous system.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation is important for the development and functioning of the nervous system.
source: Recently, missense mutations in OGT have been linked to intellectual disability, indicating that this modification is important for the development and functioning of the nervous system.
evidence: This is inferred from the link between OGT mutations and intellectual disability.

claim: Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation leads to defects in synaptogenesis in Drosophila melanogaster carrying a patient-derived OGT mutation.
source: Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation leads to defects in synaptogenesis and reduced sleep stability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NMJ phenotypes in mutant flies.

claim: Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation leads to reduced sleep stability in Drosophila melanogaster carrying a patient-derived OGT mutation.
source: Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation leads to defects in synaptogenesis and reduced sleep stability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing sleep phenotypes in mutant flies.

claim: Synaptogenesis and sleep phenotypes can be partially rescued by genetically targeting OGA.
source: Both these phenotypes can be partially rescued by genetically or chemically targeting OGA, suggesting that a balance of OGT/OGA activity is required for normal neuronal development and function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of phenotypes in OGA knockout flies.

claim: Synaptogenesis and sleep phenotypes can be partially rescued by chemically targeting OGA.
source: Both these phenotypes can be partially rescued by genetically or chemically targeting OGA, suggesting that a balance of OGT/OGA activity is required for normal neuronal development and function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of phenotypes with Thiamet G treatment.

claim: A balance of OGT/OGA activity is required for normal neuronal development and function.
source: Both these phenotypes can be partially rescued by genetically or chemically targeting OGA, suggesting that a balance of OGT/OGA activity is required for normal neuronal development and function.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that reducing OGA activity can compensate for reduced OGT activity.

claim: Intellectual disability affects around 1% of the population globally.
source: Intellectual disability (ID) is a disorder affecting around 1% of the population globally (McKenzie et al., 2016), characterised by an intelligence quotient lower than 70 accompanied by reduced adaptive behaviour (Salvador-Carulla et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McKenzie et al., 2016.

claim: Intellectual disability is characterised by an intelligence quotient lower than 70 accompanied by reduced adaptive behaviour.
source: Intellectual disability (ID) is a disorder affecting around 1% of the population globally (McKenzie et al., 2016), characterised by an intelligence quotient lower than 70 accompanied by reduced adaptive behaviour (Salvador-Carulla et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Salvador-Carulla et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations in the X chromosome gene OGT were identified as causal for intellectual disability.
source: Recently, mutations in the X chromosome gene OGT were identified as causal for ID, a condition termed OGT congenital disorder of glycosylation (OGT-CDG) (Willems et al., 2017; Pravata et al., 2020b; Pravata et al., 2019; Pravata et al., 2020a; Vaidyanathan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies identifying OGT mutations in ID patients.

claim: Patients with OGT-CDG present with diverse signs including microcephaly and white matter abnormalities.
source: Patients with OGT-CDG present with diverse signs of varying penetrance, such as microcephaly and white matter abnormalities, as well as non-neurological signs such as clinodactyly, facial dysmorphism, and developmental delay, manifesting as low birth weight and short stature (Pravata et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pravata et al., 2020b.

claim: Patients with OGT-CDG present with non-neurological signs such as clinodactyly, facial dysmorphism, and developmental delay.
source: Patients with OGT-CDG present with diverse signs of varying penetrance, such as microcephaly and white matter abnormalities, as well as non-neurological signs such as clinodactyly, facial dysmorphism, and developmental delay, manifesting as low birth weight and short stature (Pravata et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pravata et al., 2020b.

claim: Non-morphological signs of pathogenic OGT mutations include behavioural problems, sleep abnormalities, and epilepsy.
source: Beyond ID, non-morphological signs of pathogenic OGT mutations include behavioural problems as well as sleep abnormalities and epilepsy (Pravata et al., 2020b; Selvan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pravata et al., 2020b and Selvan et al., 2018.

claim: OGT is a nucleocytoplasmic glycosyltransferase composed of a tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain and a catalytic domain.
source: OGT encodes a nucleocytoplasmic glycosyltransferase, O-linked β-N-acetyl glucosamine (O-GlcNAc) transferase (OGT), a multifunctional protein composed of two domains: a tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain and a catalytic domain (Kreppel and Hart, 1999; Lubas et al., 1997; Kreppel et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kreppel and Hart, 1999; Lubas et al., 1997; Kreppel et al., 1997.

claim: Mutations affecting either the TPR or catalytic domain have been identified in patients with OGT-CDG.
source: Mutations affecting either domain have been identified in patients with OGT-CDG, though clinical manifestation of the disorder does not appear to segregate with the domain affected (Pravata et al., 2020b), suggesting a common disease mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pravata et al., 2020b.

claim: Clinical manifestation of OGT-CDG does not appear to segregate with the domain affected by mutations.
source: Mutations affecting either domain have been identified in patients with OGT-CDG, though clinical manifestation of the disorder does not appear to segregate with the domain affected (Pravata et al., 2020b), suggesting a common disease mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pravata et al., 2020b.

claim: The lack of segregation of clinical manifestation with domain affected suggests a common disease mechanism for OGT-CDG.
source: Mutations affecting either domain have been identified in patients with OGT-CDG, though clinical manifestation of the disorder does not appear to segregate with the domain affected (Pravata et al., 2020b), suggesting a common disease mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutations in different domains produce similar clinical outcomes.

claim: The N-terminal TPR domain is believed to confer substrate specificity for the glycosyltransferase function of OGT.
source: The N-terminal TPR domain is believed to confer substrate specificity for the glycosyltransferase function of OGT (Iyer and Hart, 2003; Levine et al., 2018; Clarke et al., 2008) and is important for non-catalytic functions of the protein (Urso et al., 2020; Levine et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iyer and Hart, 2003; Levine et al., 2018; Clarke et al., 2008.

claim: The TPR domain is important for non-catalytic functions of OGT.
source: The N-terminal TPR domain is believed to confer substrate specificity for the glycosyltransferase function of OGT (Iyer and Hart, 2003; Levine et al., 2018; Clarke et al., 2008) and is important for non-catalytic functions of the protein (Urso et al., 2020; Levine et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Urso et al., 2020; Levine et al., 2021.

claim: The catalytic domain of OGT transfers O-GlcNAc onto serine and threonine residues of nucleocytoplasmic proteins.
source: The catalytic domain fulfils two known functions, the transfer of O-GlcNAc onto serine and threonine residues of nucleocytoplasmic proteins (O-GlcNAcylation) Torres and Hart, 1984; Holt et al., 1987, and the proteolytic activation of Host Cell Factor 1 (HCF-1) (Capotosti et al., 2011; Lazarus et al., 2013), a known ID-associated protein (Castro and Quintana, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Torres and Hart, 1984; Holt et al., 1987.

claim: The catalytic domain of OGT catalyzes the proteolytic activation of Host Cell Factor 1 (HCF-1).
source: The catalytic domain fulfils two known functions, the transfer of O-GlcNAc onto serine and threonine residues of nucleocytoplasmic proteins (O-GlcNAcylation) Torres and Hart, 1984; Holt et al., 1987, and the proteolytic activation of Host Cell Factor 1 (HCF-1) (Capotosti et al., 2011; Lazarus et al., 2013), a known ID-associated protein (Castro and Quintana, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Capotosti et al., 2011; Lazarus et al., 2013.

claim: HCF-1 is a known ID-associated protein.
source: The catalytic domain fulfils two known functions, the transfer of O-GlcNAc onto serine and threonine residues of nucleocytoplasmic proteins (O-GlcNAcylation) Torres and Hart, 1984; Holt et al., 1987, and the proteolytic activation of Host Cell Factor 1 (HCF-1) (Capotosti et al., 2011; Lazarus et al., 2013), a known ID-associated protein (Castro and Quintana, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castro and Quintana, 2020.

claim: Not all patient OGT mutations affect HCF-1 processing in vitro or when modelled in stem cells.
source: While the latter function of OGT potentially contributes to the pathogenicity of some OGT mutations (Pravata et al., 2019), not all patient mutations have been found to affect HCF-1 processing, neither in vitro nor when modelled in stem cells (Vaidyanathan et al., 2017; Selvan et al., 2018; Omelková et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vaidyanathan et al., 2017; Selvan et al., 2018; Omelková et al., 2023.

claim: The role of altered O-GlcNAcylation in OGT-CDG pathogenicity remains an open question.
source: Overall, the role of altered O-GlcNAcylation in OGT-CDG pathogenicity remains an open question, as many of the other functions fulfilled by this protein have the potential to contribute to ID.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the complexity of OGT functions.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation is a dynamic modification occurring on around 5000 proteins in the human proteome.
source: O-GlcNAcylation is a dynamic modification occurring on around 5000 proteins in the human proteome (Wulff-Fuentes et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wulff-Fuentes et al., 2021.

claim: The dynamic nature of O-GlcNAcylation is conferred by O-GlcNAcase (OGA), which catalyses the removal of O-GlcNAc.
source: The dynamic nature of the modification is conferred by O-GlcNAcase (OGA), which opposes OGT, catalysing the removal of O-GlcNAc (Heckel et al., 1998; Gao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heckel et al., 1998; Gao et al., 2001.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation has been extensively implicated in neuronal development, functioning, and disease.
source: O-GlcNAcylation has been extensively implicated in neuronal development, functioning, and disease (Lee et al., 2021; Muha et al., 2021; Lagerlöf et al., 2017; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2017) and is therefore likely to play a key role in the pathogenicity of OGT-CDG.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on O-GlcNAcylation in neuronal contexts.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation is likely to play a key role in the pathogenicity of OGT-CDG.
source: O-GlcNAcylation has been extensively implicated in neuronal development, functioning, and disease (Lee et al., 2021; Muha et al., 2021; Lagerlöf et al., 2017; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2017) and is therefore likely to play a key role in the pathogenicity of OGT-CDG.
evidence: This is inferred from the extensive evidence linking O-GlcNAcylation to neuronal processes.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster OGT (sxc) was first studied as a Polycomb group (PcG) gene.
source: The first evidence for the requirement for OGT in development was the study of Drosophila melanogaster OGT, super sex combs (sxc), as a Polycomb group (PcG) gene, amorphic mutations of which were found to result in defects in body segment determination (Ingham, 1984), a function later ascribed to its glycosyltransferase activity (Gambetta and Müller, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ingham, 1984 and Gambetta and Müller, 2014.

claim: Amorphic mutations of sxc result in defects in body segment determination.
source: The first evidence for the requirement for OGT in development was the study of Drosophila melanogaster OGT, super sex combs (sxc), as a Polycomb group (PcG) gene, amorphic mutations of which were found to result in defects in body segment determination (Ingham, 1984), a function later ascribed to its glycosyltransferase activity (Gambetta and Müller, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ingham, 1984.

claim: The role of sxc in body segment determination is ascribed to its glycosyltransferase activity.
source: The first evidence for the requirement for OGT in development was the study of Drosophila melanogaster OGT, super sex combs (sxc), as a Polycomb group (PcG) gene, amorphic mutations of which were found to result in defects in body segment determination (Ingham, 1984), a function later ascribed to its glycosyltransferase activity (Gambetta and Müller, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gambetta and Müller, 2014.

claim: The role of O-GlcNAcylation in PcG function is important for normal neuronal development and highly sensitive to perturbations.
source: The role of O-GlcNAcylation in PcG function is known to be important for normal neuronal development and highly sensitive to perturbations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Maternal hyperglycaemia can drive increased O-GlcNAcylation in the embryo altering neuronal maturation and differentiation patterns through altered PcG function.
source: For example, maternal hyperglycaemia can drive increased O-GlcNAcylation in the embryo altering neuronal maturation and differentiation patterns through altered PcG function (Parween et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Parween et al., 2022.

claim: Multiple core developmental regulators require O-GlcNAcylation for appropriate function.
source: Multiple additional core developmental regulators have been found to require O-GlcNAcylation for appropriate function, with deregulation of the modification affecting stem cell maintenance through core pluripotency factors such as Sox2 (Kim et al., 2021a; Jang et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2016), cell fate determination through STAT3 (Fan et al., 2020), and Notch signalling (Chen et al., 2021) and neuronal morphogenesis through the protein kinase A signalling cascade (Francisco et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on various developmental regulators.

claim: Deregulation of O-GlcNAcylation affects stem cell maintenance through core pluripotency factors such as Sox2.
source: Multiple additional core developmental regulators have been found to require O-GlcNAcylation for appropriate function, with deregulation of the modification affecting stem cell maintenance through core pluripotency factors such as Sox2 (Kim et al., 2021a; Jang et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2016), cell fate determination through STAT3 (Fan et al., 2020), and Notch signalling (Chen et al., 2021) and neuronal morphogenesis through the protein kinase A signalling cascade (Francisco et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2021a; Jang et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2016.

claim: Deregulation of O-GlcNAcylation affects cell fate determination through STAT3.
source: Multiple additional core developmental regulators have been found to require O-GlcNAcylation for appropriate function, with deregulation of the modification affecting stem cell maintenance through core pluripotency factors such as Sox2 (Kim et al., 2021a; Jang et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2016), cell fate determination through STAT3 (Fan et al., 2020), and Notch signalling (Chen et al., 2021) and neuronal morphogenesis through the protein kinase A signalling cascade (Francisco et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2020.

claim: Deregulation of O-GlcNAcylation affects Notch signalling.
source: Multiple additional core developmental regulators have been found to require O-GlcNAcylation for appropriate function, with deregulation of the modification affecting stem cell maintenance through core pluripotency factors such as Sox2 (Kim et al., 2021a; Jang et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2016), cell fate determination through STAT3 (Fan et al., 2020), and Notch signalling (Chen et al., 2021) and neuronal morphogenesis through the protein kinase A signalling cascade (Francisco et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2021.

claim: Deregulation of O-GlcNAcylation affects neuronal morphogenesis through the protein kinase A signalling cascade.
source: Multiple additional core developmental regulators have been found to require O-GlcNAcylation for appropriate function, with deregulation of the modification affecting stem cell maintenance through core pluripotency factors such as Sox2 (Kim et al., 2021a; Jang et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2016), cell fate determination through STAT3 (Fan et al., 2020), and Notch signalling (Chen et al., 2021) and neuronal morphogenesis through the protein kinase A signalling cascade (Francisco et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Francisco et al., 2009.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation plays an important role in neuronal functioning related to memory formation.
source: Additionally, O-GlcNAcylation is known to play an important role in neuronal functioning related to memory formation (Muha et al., 2019; Taylor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muha et al., 2019; Taylor et al., 2014.

claim: Elevating O-GlcNAcylation in sleep-deprived zebrafish or mice can reverse memory defects associated with a lack of sleep.
source: For example, elevating O-GlcNAcylation in sleep-deprived zebrafish or mice can reverse memory defects associated with a lack of sleep (Lee et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021b.

claim: Several proteins important for memory formation are modulated by O-GlcNAcylation, such as CREB and CRMP2.
source: The extent of the role of OGT in memory formation is not fully understood, although several proteins important for this process are modulated by O-GlcNAcylation, such as CREB (Rexach et al., 2012) or CRMP2 (Muha et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rexach et al., 2012 and Muha et al., 2019.

claim: A key unanswered question regarding OGT-CDG is the contribution of developmental roles of OGT relative to its role in the functioning of the adult nervous system.
source: Therefore, a key unanswered question regarding the aetiology of OGT-CDG is the contribution of the developmental roles of OGT relative to its role in the functioning of the adult nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as a research question motivating the study.

claim: Drosophila OGT (DmOGT) is highly similar to its human ortholog, with 73% amino acid identity and a high degree of structural similarity.
source: Drosophila OGT (DmOGT) is highly similar to its human ortholog, with 73% amino acid identity and a high degree of structural similarity (Mariappa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mariappa et al., 2015.

claim: In Drosophila, OGT does not catalyse HCF-1 proteolytic activation, a function fulfilled instead by taspase 1.
source: However, in the fly OGT does not catalyse HCF-1 proteolytic activation, a function fulfilled instead by taspase 1 (Capotosti et al., 2007), eliminating this function of OGT as a confounding variable in understanding the role of O-GlcNAcylation in ID.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Capotosti et al., 2007.

claim: OGT-CDG catalytic domain mutations can reduce global O-GlcNAcylation in adult Drosophila tissue.
source: Previous work modelling OGT-CDG mutations in Drosophila has demonstrated that OGT-CDG catalytic domain mutations can reduce global O-GlcNAcylation in adult tissue (Pravata et al., 2019), which is linked with defects in habituation and synaptogenesis (Fenckova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pravata et al., 2019 and Fenckova et al., 2022.

claim: Reduced O-GlcNAcylation in Drosophila is linked with defects in habituation and synaptogenesis.
source: Previous work modelling OGT-CDG mutations in Drosophila has demonstrated that OGT-CDG catalytic domain mutations can reduce global O-GlcNAcylation in adult tissue (Pravata et al., 2019), which is linked with defects in habituation and synaptogenesis (Fenckova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fenckova et al., 2022.

claim: The C921Y mutation in OGT can reduce O-GlcNAcylation throughout development in Drosophila.
source: Here, we demonstrate that a recently discovered ID-associated catalytic domain mutation in OGT (resulting in the amino acid substitution C921Y Omelková et al., 2023) can reduce O-GlcNAcylation throughout development in Drosophila, which can be rescued by genetically or pharmacologically abolishing or reducing OGA activity, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reduced O-GlcNAcylation due to the C921Y mutation can be rescued by genetically or pharmacologically abolishing or reducing OGA activity.
source: Here, we demonstrate that a recently discovered ID-associated catalytic domain mutation in OGT (resulting in the amino acid substitution C921Y Omelková et al., 2023) can reduce O-GlcNAcylation throughout development in Drosophila, which can be rescued by genetically or pharmacologically abolishing or reducing OGA activity, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: sxc mutations have a strong effect on larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) development.
source: We find a strong effect of sxc mutations on larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) development, which can be partially reversed by inhibiting or abolishing OGA catalytic activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NMJ phenotypes in mutant larvae.

claim: The effect of sxc mutations on NMJ development can be partially reversed by inhibiting or abolishing OGA catalytic activity.
source: We find a strong effect of sxc mutations on larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) development, which can be partially reversed by inhibiting or abolishing OGA catalytic activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of NMJ phenotypes.

claim: A catalytic domain mutation in sxc can negatively impact sleep, reducing sleep bout duration.
source: Additionally, we demonstrate that a catalytic domain mutation in sxc can negatively impact sleep, reducing sleep bout duration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing sleep phenotypes in mutant flies.

claim: The sleep phenotype caused by a catalytic domain mutation in sxc can be rescued by abolishing OGA activity.
source: This phenotype can be rescued by abolishing OGA activity and partially reversed by inhibiting OGA in adulthood, suggesting that some aspects of OGT-CDG may not be developmental in origin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of sleep phenotypes.

claim: The sleep phenotype caused by a catalytic domain mutation in sxc can be partially reversed by inhibiting OGA in adulthood.
source: This phenotype can be rescued by abolishing OGA activity and partially reversed by inhibiting OGA in adulthood, suggesting that some aspects of OGT-CDG may not be developmental in origin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing partial rescue of sleep phenotypes with adult OGA inhibition.

claim: Some aspects of OGT-CDG may not be developmental in origin.
source: This phenotype can be rescued by abolishing OGA activity and partially reversed by inhibiting OGA in adulthood, suggesting that some aspects of OGT-CDG may not be developmental in origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that adult OGA inhibition can partially rescue phenotypes.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation in lysates from adult heads was significantly reduced in the sxcN595K mutant compared to a control genotype.
source: Consistent with previous reports, O-GlcNAcylation in lysates from adult heads was found to be significantly reduced in the sxcN595K mutant compared to a control genotype (Figure 1A; Pravata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and cited previous work.

claim: The sxcC941Y mutant strain presented with a significantly more severe reduction in global O-GlcNAcylation than sxcN595K, to roughly 40% of the control genotype.
source: The newly generated sxcC941Y mutant strain presented with a significantly more severe reduction in global O-GlcNAcylation, to roughly 40% of the control genotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The reduction in O-GlcNAcylation in sxcC941Y was observed despite a modest, yet significant, increase in OGT protein relative to the control genotype.
source: This reduction in O-GlcNAcylation was observed despite a modest, yet significant, increase in OGT protein relative to the control genotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The sxcK872M genotype was previously found to be recessive lethal at the late pupal stages.
source: The sxcK872M genotype was previously found to be recessive lethal at the late pupal stages (Mariappa et al., 2018); therefore, for this genotype O-GlcNAcylation and OGT levels were only assayed at embryonic and larval stages.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mariappa et al., 2018.

claim: Both sxcC941Y and sxcK872M stage 16–17 embryos present with significantly reduced O-GlcNAcylation and increased OGT.
source: Both sxcC941Y and sxcK872M stage 16–17 embryos present with significantly reduced O-GlcNAcylation and increased OGT (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation seen in sxcK872M embryos is likely largely due to maternally contributed wildtype sxc gene product.
source: As sxcK872M embryos were derived from heterozygous parents, O-GlcNAcylation seen in these embryos is likely largely due to maternally contributed wildtype sxc gene product (Ingham, 1984; Sinclair et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic cross design and supported by citations.

claim: By the third-instar larval stage, sxcK872M larvae present with significantly lower O-GlcNAcylation than both the control and sxcC941Y genotype.
source: By the third-instar larval stage of development, the difference in O-GlcNAcylation between the sxcC941Y and sxcK872M genotypes is more pronounced. sxcK872M larvae present with significantly lower O-GlcNAcylation than both the control and sxcC941Y genotype (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation in the sxcC941Y larvae remains significantly reduced relative to the control genotype at the third-instar larval stage.
source: O-GlcNAcylation in the sxcC941Y larvae remains significantly reduced relative to the control genotype, as at all other stages of development assayed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the third-instar larval stage, sxcC941Y larvae do not present with significantly elevated DmOGT protein levels.
source: Surprisingly, at this stage of development, sxcC941Y larvae do not present with significantly elevated DmOGT protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mean DmOGT protein levels in sxcK872M larvae are over eight times higher than in the control genotype.
source: Strikingly, the mean DmOGT protein levels in sxcK872M larvae are over eight times higher than in the control genotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: sxcC941Y flies present with an increased penetrance of ectopic bristles on the scutellum, with 31% presenting with one or more additional bristles.
source: sxcC941Y flies were found to also present with an increased penetrance of ectopic bristles on the scutellum, with 31% of sxcC941Y flies presenting with one or more additional bristles, while in the control genotype this only occurred in 8% of flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the control genotype, ectopic scutellar bristles only occurred in 8% of flies.
source: sxcC941Y flies were found to also present with an increased penetrance of ectopic bristles on the scutellum, with 31% of sxcC941Y flies presenting with one or more additional bristles, while in the control genotype this only occurred in 8% of flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knocking out OGA led to a marked increase in O-GlcNAcylation in lysates from adult heads in the sxcC941Y line, above levels seen in the control genotype.
source: When assayed by Western blot, we found that knocking out OGA led to a marked increase in O-GlcNAcylation in lysates from adult heads in the sxcC941Y line, above levels seen in the control genotype (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Despite the OgaKO allele having no effect on its own, sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies had an increased penetrance of ectopic scutellar bristles beyond what was observed for sxcC941Y flies.
source: Surprisingly, we found that despite the OgaKO allele having no effect on its own, sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies had an increased penetrance of ectopic scutellar bristles beyond what we observed for sxcC941Y flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Global O-GlcNAcylation was rescued to control levels in sxcC941Y flies fed 3 mM TMG for 72 hr.
source: After assaying varying concentrations of OGA inhibitor, we found that global O-GlcNAcylation was rescued to control levels in sxcC941Y flies fed 3 mM TMG for 72 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A higher 5 mM concentration of TMG did not rescue O-GlcNAcylation to control levels in sxcC941Y flies.
source: Paradoxically, a higher 5 mM concentration did not have the same effect. Flies fed this higher concentration of TMG were found to have significantly decreased global O-GlcNAcylation relative to the control genotype, though this appeared to be due to an alteration in the pattern of O-GlcNAcylation with some substrates retaining elevated O-GlcNAcylation relative to sxcC941Y flies fed standard food (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TMG treatment resulted in decreased levels of DmOGT in sxcC941Y flies.
source: Accompanying elevated O-GlcNAcylation, TMG treatment resulted in decreased levels of DmOGT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For sxcC941Y flies fed 3 mM TMG, DmOGT protein levels were rescued to control levels.
source: For sxcC941Y flies fed 3 mM TMG, DmOGT protein levels were rescued to control levels, while for flies fed 5 mM TMG, DmOGT decreased below levels seen in the control genotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For sxcC941Y flies fed 5 mM TMG, DmOGT decreased below levels seen in the control genotype.
source: For sxcC941Y flies fed 3 mM TMG, DmOGT protein levels were rescued to control levels, while for flies fed 5 mM TMG, DmOGT decreased below levels seen in the control genotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TMG concentrations required to rescue O-GlcNAcylation during the larval stages of development were much lower than for adults.
source: Presumably due to differences in feeding behaviour, TMG concentrations required to rescue O-GlcNAcylation during the larval stages of development were much lower than for adults.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of effective TMG concentrations in adults vs. larvae.

claim: At 150 μM TMG, O-GlcNAcylation in sxcC941Y larvae was no longer significantly different from the control genotype.
source: At 150 μM TMG, O-GlcNAcylation in sxcC941Y larvae was no longer significantly different from the control genotype, while O-GlcNAcylation in larvae fed 200 μM TMG was both significantly higher than in the sxcC941Y larvae fed standard food and not significantly different from the control genotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation in larvae fed 200 μM TMG was both significantly higher than in the sxcC941Y larvae fed standard food and not significantly different from the control genotype.
source: At 150 μM TMG, O-GlcNAcylation in sxcC941Y larvae was no longer significantly different from the control genotype, while O-GlcNAcylation in larvae fed 200 μM TMG was both significantly higher than in the sxcC941Y larvae fed standard food and not significantly different from the control genotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The average NMJ area in sxcWT larvae was significantly higher than in both sxcC941Y and sxcK872M mutant larvae.
source: The average NMJ area in sxcWT larvae (mean ± standard deviation, 326 ± 52 μm2) was significantly higher than in both sxcC941Y (278 ± 28 μm2) and sxcK872M mutant larvae (198 ± 32 μm2), with a significant difference between the two sxc mutant groups.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NMJ area was partially rescued in the sxcC941Y;OgaKO line relative to the control genotype.
source: This phenotype was partially rescued in the sxcC941Y;OgaKO line (291 ± 39 μm2), relative to the control genotype, although the total area of the NMJs was not affected in the OgaKO larvae (337 ± 32 μm2), consistent with previous research on OgaKO larvae (Fenckova et al., 2022; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and cited previous work.

claim: The total area of the NMJs was not affected in the OgaKO larvae.
source: This phenotype was partially rescued in the sxcC941Y;OgaKO line (291 ± 39 μm2), relative to the control genotype, although the total area of the NMJs was not affected in the OgaKO larvae (337 ± 32 μm2), consistent with previous research on OgaKO larvae (Fenckova et al., 2022; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and cited previous work.

claim: Total NMJ length was significantly different between the control genotype and sxcC941Y and sxcK872M larvae.
source: Total length was also significantly different between the control genotype (mean ± standard deviation, 115 ± 18 μm) and sxcC941Y (93 ± 11 μm) and sxcK872M larvae (74 ± 7 μm).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NMJ length was partially rescued in sxcC941Y;OgaKO larvae relative to sxcWT larvae.
source: This parameter was also partially rescued in sxcC941Y;OgaKO larvae (102 ± 14 μm) relative to sxcWT larvae, while being unaffected in the OgaKO genotype (115 ± 13 μm) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NMJ length was unaffected in the OgaKO genotype.
source: This parameter was also partially rescued in sxcC941Y;OgaKO larvae (102 ± 14 μm) relative to sxcWT larvae, while being unaffected in the OgaKO genotype (115 ± 13 μm) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Bouton numbers were significantly reduced in both sxcC941Y and sxcK872M larvae, relative to the sxcWT controls.
source: Finally, bouton numbers were also significantly reduced in both sxcC941Y (mean ± standard deviation, 15 ± 3) and sxcK872M (12 ± 1) larvae, relative to the sxcWT controls (19 ± 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Bouton number remained significantly reduced in the sxcC941Y;OgaKO line relative to the control genotype.
source: Unlike total area and length, this parameter remained significantly reduced in the sxcC941Y;OgaKO line (16 ± 2) relative to the control genotype (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No significant difference in muscle size was observed between sxcWT and sxcK872M larvae.
source: No significant difference in muscle size was observed between sxcWT and sxcK872M larvae, and when NMJ area was normalised to muscle area, this parameter remained significantly reduced in sxcK872M larvae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When NMJ area was normalised to muscle area, this parameter remained significantly reduced in sxcK872M larvae.
source: No significant difference in muscle size was observed between sxcWT and sxcK872M larvae, and when NMJ area was normalised to muscle area, this parameter remained significantly reduced in sxcK872M larvae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of wild type sxc in sxcK872M larval neurons could significantly increase NMJ total area, but not length or bouton number.
source: This demonstrated that overexpression of wild type sxc in sxcK872M larval neurons could significantly increase NMJ total area, but not length or bouton number.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of wild type sxc in muscle cells did not lead to any significant effect on NMJ morphology.
source: By contrast, similar overexpression in muscle cells did not lead to any significant effect on NMJ morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The sxcH596F mutation results in a significant decrease in NMJ area relative to the control genotype.
source: We found that this mutation also results in a significant decrease in NMJ area (mean ± standard deviation, 260 ± 23 μm2) relative to the control genotype (304 ± 18 μm2), with a similar effect for length and bouton number, consistent with the other genotypes assayed here (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: The total NMJ area in sxcC941Y larvae treated with 200 μM TMG was no longer significantly different relative to the control genotype.
source: The total NMJ area in sxcC941Y larvae treated with 200 μM TMG (mean ± standard deviation, 303 ± 40 μm2) was no longer significantly different relative to the control genotype (319 ± 31 μm2) while sxcC941Y fed a vehicle control presented with reduced NMJ area relative to the control genotype (272 + 40 μm2) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: sxcC941Y larvae fed a vehicle control presented with reduced NMJ area relative to the control genotype.
source: The total NMJ area in sxcC941Y larvae treated with 200 μM TMG (mean ± standard deviation, 303 ± 40 μm2) was no longer significantly different relative to the control genotype (319 ± 31 μm2) while sxcC941Y fed a vehicle control presented with reduced NMJ area relative to the control genotype (272 + 40 μm2) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TMG inhibition in sxcC941Y larvae did not significantly rescue NMJ length relative to the control genotype.
source: Unlike in sxcC941Y;OgaKO larvae, TMG inhibition in sxcC941Y larvae did not significantly rescue NMJ length (median ± interquartile range, 106 ± 13 μm) relative to the control genotype (117 ± 9 μm), although a non-significant increase in length relative to sxcC941Y larvae fed a vehicle was observed (95 μm ± 8) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: sxcC941Y larvae fed 200 μM TMG presented with significantly fewer boutons per NMJ relative to the control genotype.
source: Similar to the OGA knockout experiment (Figure 3D), sxcC941Y larvae fed 200 μM TMG presented with significantly fewer boutons per NMJ (mean ± standard deviation, 16 ± 2) relative to the control genotype (19 ± 2) without a significant difference relative to the sxcC941Y larvae fed a vehicle control (15 ± 2) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Total activity of sxcC941Y flies was not significantly different from the control genotype.
source: Total activity of sxcC941Y flies (median ± interquartile range, 1.25e3 ± 6.6e2 counts/24 hr) was not significantly different from the control genotype (1.23e3 ± 5.8e2 counts/24 hr).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies were significantly less active than the control genotype.
source: However, sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies were significantly less active than the control genotype (8.9e2 ± 3.9e2 counts/24 hr), despite the OgaKO allele having no effect on total activity on its own (1.13e3 ± 5.7e2 counts/24 hr) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The OgaKO allele had no effect on total activity on its own.
source: However, sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies were significantly less active than the control genotype (8.9e2 ± 3.9e2 counts/24 hr), despite the OgaKO allele having no effect on total activity on its own (1.13e3 ± 5.7e2 counts/24 hr) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: sxcC941Y flies presented with reduced total sleep relative to the control genotype.
source: By contrast, sxcC941Y flies did present with reduced total sleep (mean ± standard deviation, 8.1e2 ± 1.8e2 min/24 hr), relative to the control genotype (9.4e2 ± 1.4e2 min/24 hr), which was rescued in sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies to wild type levels (9.7e2 ± 1.3e2 min/24 hr) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Total sleep was rescued in sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies to wild type levels.
source: By contrast, sxcC941Y flies did present with reduced total sleep (mean ± standard deviation, 8.1e2 ± 1.8e2 min/24 hr), relative to the control genotype (9.4e2 ± 1.4e2 min/24 hr), which was rescued in sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies to wild type levels (9.7e2 ± 1.3e2 min/24 hr) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The nature of sleep disruption in the OGT-CDG flies was due to a reduced duration of individual sleep bouts both during the day and night.
source: Upon more detailed investigation, the nature of sleep disruption in the OGT-CDG flies was found to be due to a reduced duration of individual sleep bouts both during the day and night in these flies (median ± interquartile range, 28 ± 13 min and 39 ± 30 min, respectively) compared to the control genotype (42 ± 22 min and 75 ± 56 min, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mean sleep bout duration in sxcC941Y flies is partially rescued by knocking out Oga both during the day and at night.
source: Mean sleep bout duration in sxcC941Y flies is partially rescued by elevating global O-GlcNAcylation through knocking out Oga both during the day (32 ± 19 min) and at night (56 ± 40 min), although during both time periods sleep bout duration remained significantly reduced compared to the control genotype (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: sxcWT flies experience significantly more sleep bouts longer than 2 hr relative to sxcC941Y flies.
source: sxcWT flies experience significantly more sleep bouts longer than 2 hr (median ± interquartile range 2.0 ± 1.0 bouts/24 hr) relative to sxcC941Y flies (1 ± 1.3 bouts).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The number of sleep bouts longer than 2 hr is rescued by knocking out Oga in sxcC941Y flies.
source: This aspect of sleep is also rescued by knocking out Oga, with sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies no longer presenting with a significant decrease in number of sleep bouts longer than 2 hr (1.7 ± 1.3 bouts/24 hr) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: sxcC941Y and sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies present with significantly more frequent sleep bouts during the day and at night compared to the control genotype.
source: Accompanying decreased sleep bout duration, sxcC941Y and sxcC941Y;OgaKO flies present with significantly more frequent sleep bouts during the day (mean ± standard deviation 13 ± 3 and 14 ± 5 bouts, respectively) and at night (14 ± 5 and 13 ± 5 bouts, respectively), compared to the control genotype (day: 11 ± 4 and night: 9 ± 4 bouts, respectively) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Adult sxcC941Y flies fed 3 mM TMG for 72 hr no longer presented with decreased overall sleep duration.
source: Adult sxcC941Y flies were fed 3 mM TMG for 72 hr prior to and during activity monitoring. In this condition, OGT-CDG flies no longer presented with decreased overall sleep duration (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mean sleep duration and daily number of sleep bouts longer than 2 hr remained significantly reduced in sxcC941Y flies fed 3 mM TMG compared to the sxcWT control.
source: However, other aspects of sleep remained disrupted in OGT-CDG flies. Both mean sleep duration (median ± interquartile range, day: 22 ± 10 min, night: 44 ± 26 min) and daily number of sleep bouts longer than 2 hr (median ± interquartile range, 1 ± 1 bouts/24 hr) remained significantly reduced compared to the sxcWT control (day: 28 ± 13 min, night: 50 ± 43, 1.3 ± 1.0 bouts/24 hr, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6D.

claim: sxcC941Y flies presented with significantly more sleep bouts throughout the day than the control genotype.
source: Additionally, as in previous experiments, sxcC941Y flies presented with significantly more sleep bouts throughout the day (mean ± standard deviation, day: 17 ± 4 bouts, night: 15 ± 5 bouts) than the control genotype (day: 14 ± 4 bouts, night: 12 ± 4 bouts) (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mean sleep bout duration in sxcC941Y flies fed TMG was no longer significantly different from the control genotype both during the day and at night.
source: Interestingly, these phenotypes were partially reversed by TMG feeding. Mean sleep bout duration in sxcC941Y flies fed TMG was no longer significantly different from the control genotype both during the day and at night (26 ± 13 min and 44 ± 39 min, respectively), nor was the number of sleep bouts longer than 2 hr (1.3 ± 1.0 bouts/24 hr).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The number of sleep bouts longer than 2 hr in sxcC941Y flies fed TMG was no longer significantly different from the control genotype.
source: Interestingly, these phenotypes were partially reversed by TMG feeding. Mean sleep bout duration in sxcC941Y flies fed TMG was no longer significantly different from the control genotype both during the day and at night (26 ± 13 min and 44 ± 39 min, respectively), nor was the number of sleep bouts longer than 2 hr (1.3 ± 1.0 bouts/24 hr).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The number of sleep bouts in sxcC941Y flies fed TMG was no longer significantly different than for the control genotype fed a vehicle control.
source: The number of sleep bouts in sxcC941Y flies fed TMG was also no longer significantly different than for the control genotype fed a vehicle control (day: 16 ± 3 bouts, night: 13 ± 4 bouts), although it remained non-significantly elevated relative to the control genotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Neither genotype nor inclusion of TMG in food influenced total feeding.
source: This rescue was not due to non-specific effects of TMG on feeding behaviour, such as aversion due to altered food taste, as neither genotype nor inclusion of TMG in food influenced total feeding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Effects of OGT-CDG mutations may not be solely developmental, and defective O-GlcNAc cycling in adulthood may be an important contributor to the pathogenesis of these mutations.
source: These results suggest that effects of OGT-CDG mutations may not be solely developmental, and that defective O-GlcNAc cycling in adulthood may be an important contributor to the pathogenesis of these mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that adult OGA inhibition can partially rescue phenotypes.

claim: Glial knockdown of sxc resulted in a significant decrease in total daily sleep relative to GAL4 and UAS controls.
source: Conversely, knockdown of sxc in glial cells resulted in a significant decrease in total daily sleep (median ± interquartile range, 690 ± 230 min/24 hr), relative to a GAL4 (800 ± 170 min/24 hr), and UAS control (960 ± 120 min/24 hr) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Glial knockdown of sxc caused a decrease in the mean duration of sleep episodes compared with control genotypes.
source: As in sxcC941Y flies, glial knockdown caused a decrease in the mean duration of sleep episodes (median ± interquartile range, day: 29 ± 26 min, night: 31 ± 19 min) compared with the control GAL4 (day: 38 ± 32 min, night: 46 ± 26 min) and UAS genotypes (day: 39 ± 24 min, night: 57 ± 40 min, Figure 7B); however, this effect is only significant during the night.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The number of sleep bouts was not significantly increased in flies expressing sxc RNAi in glial cells relative to either control.
source: Unlike in OGT-CDG flies, the number of sleep bouts was not significantly increased in flies expressing sxc RNAi in glial cells (mean ± standard deviation, day: 12 ± 6 bouts, night: 13 ± 5 bouts) relative to either control (GAL4: day: 12 ± 6 bouts, night: 11 ± 5 bouts, UAS: day: 12 ± 4 bouts, night: 10 ± 4 bouts; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Flies expressing sxc RNAi in glial cells presented with fewer sleep bouts longer than 2 hr relative to the UAS control group but not the repo GAL4 line.
source: Flies expressing sxc RNAi in glial cells presented with fewer sleep bouts longer than 2 hr (median ± interquartile range, 1.0 ± 1.3 bouts/24 hr), however, only relative to the UAS control group (2 ± 0.7 bouts/24 hr) and not the repo GAL4 line (1.3 ± 0.7 bouts/24 hr) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Many mutations in OGT causal in ID do not result in a decrease in global O-GlcNAcylation in embryonic stem cells or patient derived fibroblasts.
source: Many mutations in OGT causal in ID modelled previously do not result in a decrease in global O-GlcNAcylation either in embryonic stem cells or patient derived fibroblasts, in many cases due to feedback mechanisms reducing OGA protein levels (Willems et al., 2017; Pravata et al., 2019; Selvan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Willems et al., 2017; Pravata et al., 2019; Selvan et al., 2018.

claim: The cysteine to tyrosine substitution modelled here is one of only two patient mutations which has been shown to reduce global O-GlcNAcylation when introduced in mammalian cells.
source: The cysteine to tyrosine substitution modelled here is one of only two patient mutations which has been shown to reduce global O-GlcNAcylation when introduced in mammalian cells (Pravata et al., 2020a; Omelková et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pravata et al., 2020a; Omelková et al., 2023.

claim: When modelled in mouse embryonic stem cells, the C921Y mutation results in an increase in OGT protein levels.
source: When modelled in mouse embryonic stem cells, this mutation (C921Y in humans and mice) also results in an increase in OGT protein levels (Omelková et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Omelková et al., 2023.

claim: Increased DmOGT protein levels appear to be a response commonly associated with decreased OGT catalytic activity in the fly.
source: However, in the fly, increased DmOGT protein levels appear to be a response commonly associated with decreased OGT catalytic activity, demonstrated here by the sxcK872M mutant stain and in previous work (Pravata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Pravata et al., 2019.

claim: Some evidence exists for post-transcriptional regulation of sxc expression through alternate splicing.
source: While this increase in DmOGT protein levels was not explored in further detail, some evidence exists for post-transcriptional regulation of sxc expression through alternate splicing (Ashton-Beaucage et al., 2010), a mechanism known be involved in the control of OGT and OGA expression and O-GlcNAc homeostasis in mammalian cells (Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ashton-Beaucage et al., 2010 and Tan et al., 2020.

claim: Alternate splicing is a mechanism known to be involved in the control of OGT and OGA expression and O-GlcNAc homeostasis in mammalian cells.
source: While this increase in DmOGT protein levels was not explored in further detail, some evidence exists for post-transcriptional regulation of sxc expression through alternate splicing (Ashton-Beaucage et al., 2010), a mechanism known be involved in the control of OGT and OGA expression and O-GlcNAc homeostasis in mammalian cells (Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2020.

claim: The development of scutellar bristles (macrochaetae) is well studied, particularly in the context of cell fate determination by lateral inhibition through Notch signalling.
source: Also known as macrochaetae, the development of these sensory cells is well studied, particularly in the context of cell fate determination by lateral inhibition through Notch signalling (Parks et al., 1997), providing a tractable system for the understanding of the impacts of hypo-O-GlcNAcylation on cell fate determination.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Parks et al., 1997.

claim: Notch signalling requires appropriate O-GlcNAcylation.
source: With reports of Notch signalling requiring appropriate O-GlcNAcylation (Chen et al., 2021), this phenotype presents an interesting system to research the contribution of the Notch signalling pathway to ID.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2021.

claim: Normal global O-GlcNAcylation levels can be restored in sxcC941Y adult flies through knockout of Oga.
source: Here, we show that normal global O-GlcNAcylation levels can be restored in sxcC941Y adult flies through knockout out of Oga.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: OgaKO alleles can rescue phenotypes associated with reduced O-GlcNAcylation.
source: Previous research has demonstrated that OgaKO alleles can rescue phenotypes associated with reduced O-GlcNAcylation (Fenckova et al., 2022); however, here we present the first direct evidence that global O-GlcNAcylation can exceed control levels in DmOGT hypomorphic flies in the absence of OGA.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fenckova et al., 2022.

claim: This study presents the first direct evidence that global O-GlcNAcylation can exceed control levels in DmOGT hypomorphic flies in the absence of OGA.
source: Previous research has demonstrated that OgaKO alleles can rescue phenotypes associated with reduced O-GlcNAcylation (Fenckova et al., 2022); however, here we present the first direct evidence that global O-GlcNAcylation can exceed control levels in DmOGT hypomorphic flies in the absence of OGA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The dysregulation of the ratio of stoichiometries of modification of specific substrates may be exacerbated in the absence of OGA.
source: While we did not see a concomitant rescue of the scutellar bristle phenotype seen in sxcC941Y flies, this may occur as a consequence of unique kinetics of O-GlcNAcylation and removal of O-GlcNAc on various DmOGT substrates, that is, the dysregulation of the ratio of stoichiometries of modification of specific substrates may be exacerbated in the absence of OGA.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible explanation for the lack of rescue of the scutellar bristle phenotype.

claim: Some O-GlcNAcylated proteins are not affected by OGA inhibition in cancer cells.
source: Previous research has demonstrated this may occur in mammalian cells, with some O-GlcNAcylated proteins not affected by OGA inhibition in cancer cells (Hahne et al., 2013; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hahne et al., 2013; Li et al., 2019.

claim: Both the addition and timely removal of O-GlcNAc from specific proteins may be required for normal scutellar bristle development.
source: Alternatively, it may be that both the addition and timely removal of O-GlcNAc from specific proteins is required for normal scutellar bristle development.
evidence: This is speculated as an alternative explanation for the lack of rescue of the scutellar bristle phenotype.

claim: Pharmacological approaches to inhibit OGA offer more precise control over the degree of O-GlcNAcase activity than complete ablation of Oga expression.
source: Complete ablation of Oga expression is a blunt approach, elevating O-GlcNAcylation levels beyond those seen in the control genotype and is not a feasible therapeutic approach. Pharmacological approaches to inhibit OGA offer more precise control over the degree of O-GlcNAcase activity and are being actively pursued as potential treatments for neurodegenerative disorders (Bartolomé-Nebreda et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for using pharmacological approaches and supported by a citation.

claim: Pharmacological approaches to inhibit OGA are being actively pursued as potential treatments for neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Complete ablation of Oga expression is a blunt approach, elevating O-GlcNAcylation levels beyond those seen in the control genotype and is not a feasible therapeutic approach. Pharmacological approaches to inhibit OGA offer more precise control over the degree of O-GlcNAcase activity and are being actively pursued as potential treatments for neurodegenerative disorders (Bartolomé-Nebreda et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bartolomé-Nebreda et al., 2021.

claim: TMG can be used to rescue global O-GlcNAcylation levels in sxcC941Y flies to those of a genetic background control, at various stages of development.
source: Our experiments suggest that the potent OGA inhibitor TMG can be used to rescue global O-GlcNAcylation levels in sxcC941Y flies to those of a genetic background control, at various stages of development.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rescuing O-GlcNAcylation levels through OGA inhibition also restored OGT levels in sxcC941Y flies.
source: Interestingly, rescuing O-GlcNAcylation levels through OGA inhibition also restored OGT levels in sxcC941Y flies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a clear difference in the pattern of O-GlcNAcylation visualised by immunoblotting in adult sxcC941Y flies fed TMG relative to the control genotype.
source: However, there is a clear difference in the pattern of O-GlcNAcylation visualised by immunoblotting in adult sxcC941Y flies fed TMG relative to the control genotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mechanisms controlling OGT expression in response to O-GlcNAcylation levels are particularly sensitive to OGA activity.
source: This potentially indicates that mechanisms controlling OGT expression in response to O-GlcNAcylation levels are particularly sensitive to OGA activity, lowering OGT protein levels prior to O-GlcNAcylation stoichiometry rising on some OGT substrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of paradoxical effects at higher TMG concentrations.

claim: Previous research has shown that alleles encoding hypomorphic variants of DmOGT result in overgrowth at the NMJ.
source: Previous research has shown that alleles encoding hypomorphic variants of DmOGT result in overgrowth at the NMJ, and that TPR domain mutations modelling those seen in patients result in a similar phenotype (Fenckova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fenckova et al., 2022.

claim: TPR domain mutations modelling those seen in patients result in NMJ overgrowth.
source: Previous research has shown that alleles encoding hypomorphic variants of DmOGT result in overgrowth at the NMJ, and that TPR domain mutations modelling those seen in patients result in a similar phenotype (Fenckova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fenckova et al., 2022.

claim: The sxcH596F mutation results in stunted growth at the NMJ.
source: This discrepancy is unlikely to be caused by allele-specific effects as this hypothesis was tested by assaying NMJ parameters in one of the hypomorphic mutants previously described and finding that this mutation (sxcH596F) also results in stunted growth at the NMJ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Knocking out Oga can partially rescue phenotypes at the NMJ caused by reduced OGT catalytic activity.
source: Nonetheless, as in previous research on the effects of reduced OGT catalytic activity on NMJ morphology, knocking out Oga can partially rescue phenotypes at this type of synapse (Fenckova et al., 2022), while a lack of Oga on its own does not affect NMJ morphology.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Fenckova et al., 2022.

claim: A lack of Oga on its own does not affect NMJ morphology.
source: Nonetheless, as in previous research on the effects of reduced OGT catalytic activity on NMJ morphology, knocking out Oga can partially rescue phenotypes at this type of synapse (Fenckova et al., 2022), while a lack of Oga on its own does not affect NMJ morphology.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Fenckova et al., 2022.

claim: Previous research on the role of Oga in axonal outgrowth at the larval NMJ is contradictory.
source: Previous research on the role of Oga in axonal outgrowth at the larval NMJ is contradictory, with one report indicating a lack of functional OGA protein increases NMJ morphological parameters such as area and another suggesting no effect on NMJ growth in the absence of OGA (Muha et al., 2020Fenckova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muha et al., 2020 and Fenckova et al., 2022.

claim: The NMJ phenotype caused by loss of normal O-GlcNAcylation can be partially rescued through pharmacological means, through the use of TMG.
source: This phenotype can also be partially rescued through pharmacological means, through the use of TMG.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pharmacological intervention in OGT-CDG is possible.
source: This could serve as proof of principle that pharmacological intervention in OGT-CDG is possible.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful rescue of NMJ phenotypes with TMG.

claim: Alternate mechanisms may impair bouton addition (which may also affect NMJ length) and overall NMJ area.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the NMJ phenotype caused by loss of normal O-GlcNAcylation is complex, and that potentially alternate mechanisms impair bouton addition (which may also affect NMJ length) and overall NMJ area, as the latter is more amenable to rescue across various approaches.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential rescue of NMJ parameters.

claim: Normal O-GlcNAc cycling is required for maintenance of sleep in adult flies.
source: We also demonstrate a novel behavioural effect resulting from catalytic domain mutations in sxc. Normal O-GlcNAc cycling is required for maintenance of sleep in adult flies, and reduced DmOGT catalytic activity as a result of an OGT-CDG mutation results in shorter, more frequent sleep episodes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A patient with OGT-CDG was reported to suffer from sleep disturbances characterised by abnormal EEG during sleep and insomnia.
source: Previously, a patient with this condition was reported to suffer from sleep disturbances characterised by abnormal EEG during sleep and insomnia (Selvan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Selvan et al., 2018.

claim: Normal sleep is required for multiple cognitive processes, such as memory formation, both in flies and humans.
source: This is particularly relevant given that normal sleep is required for multiple cognitive processes, such as memory formation, both in flies and humans (Ly et al., 2018; Berry et al., 2015; Rasch and Born, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ly et al., 2018; Berry et al., 2015; Rasch and Born, 2013.

claim: The sleep phenotype in OGT-CDG flies can be partially rescued by knocking out OGA or by pharmacologically elevating O-GlcNAcylation in adult flies.
source: Encouragingly, this phenotype can be partially rescued by knocking out OGA or by pharmacologically elevating O-GlcNAcylation in adult flies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of OGT catalytic activity may interact with environmental factors such as dietary composition.
source: While not directly comparable, this may suggest that loss of OGT catalytic activity interacts with environmental factors such as dietary composition.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sleep phenotypes varied with food type.

claim: Knocking down sxc in glial cells can result in a similar phenotype as the OGT-CDG mutation.
source: Further investigation revealed that knocking down sxc in glial cells can result in a similar phenotype as the OGT-CDG mutation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: This study provides the first evidence for the potential involvement of non-neuronal cell types in OGT-CDG.
source: While this does not rule out the involvement of neuronal cell types in this phenotype, the results presented here provide the first evidence for the potential involvement of non-neuronal cell types in OGT-CDG.
evidence: This is inferred from the glial knockdown experiments.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that suggests that OGT-CDG is not purely developmental and may be amenable to therapeutic approaches at later stages of life.
source: Overall, these results could have important implications for our understanding of OGT-CDG, providing the first evidence that suggests that the disorder is not purely developmental and may be amenable to therapeutic approaches at later stages of life.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that adult OGA inhibition can partially rescue phenotypes.
